prize_parts.citation: for the theory and experimental realisation of circuit quantum electrodynamics, strong coupling of superconducting circuits to single microwave photons

statement.case_for: Circuit QED is a single, sharply defined idea with a clean theory-plus-experiment attribution: Blais (with Huang, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf) proposed the architecture in 2004, and Wallraff and Schoelkopf delivered the strong-coupling experiments the same year. It has been reproduced and extended for more than twenty years, and its formalism (dispersive readout, resonator-mediated coupling, bus architecture) is now the standard language of superconducting quantum technology. Its originality is not in doubt, the interpretation is stable, and the credited trio fits the three-laureate limit without forcing out anyone who is indispensable. It is also the item on which the committee shows the broadest support: seven of eight members rank it in their top four or higher, which I treat only as a weak signal but which suggests that few colleagues would regard it as an unsafe choice.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in superconducting circuits. If the committee reads that award as having already honoured superconducting quantum circuits, a second prize in the same neighbourhood so soon looks repetitive, and the field could be seen as over-represented relative to other areas. There is also a real attribution problem: the credit for strong coupling and for the later transmon and qubit-design lines is shared with Girvin, Huang, Devoret and others who are outside the three names, so any trio leaves out people who made decisive contributions. A fair reading is that the achievement is more technology-defining than question-answering, and I weigh that against it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked circuit QED only eighth and noted that other superconducting-circuit pioneers were honoured in 2025, which may overlap with and complicate this configuration. He put the experimental Higgs discovery first, as the remaining half of the electroweak symmetry-breaking story.
responses.response: I take the overlap point seriously, but I think the 2025 prize recognised a different result: observation of quantum behaviour (tunnelling, level quantisation) in a macroscopic circuit, whereas circuit QED is about engineered strong light-matter coupling and control, which is what makes the circuits usable as quantum processors. The two are connected but not the same discovery. On the Higgs, I agree about importance and put it second, but I cannot see how to give three names a defensible share of work done by two collaborations of thousands. Whether to credit Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, or Gianotti, or the founders versus the spokespersons at announcement, is a judgement the evidence in front of us does not settle, and I would not want to force it. That ambiguity, not the science, is why I place it behind circuit QED.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, stressing that a continuum-model flat-band prediction at a specific magic angle was followed by an experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, and rated circuit QED fourth, with some doubt that a further circuit prize is needed after 2025.
responses.response: The prediction-then-observation structure is indeed an attractive feature, and I can see why a theorist of electronic structure finds it compelling. My reservations are two. First, the first author of the decisive 2018 experiments, Yuan Cao, is not among the credited names, so the experimental attribution is weaker than for circuit QED, where Wallraff and Schoelkopf led the experiments themselves. Second, the origin of the superconducting and correlated states is still debated and the field is young; I would rather see the mechanism better understood before honouring it. If the committee did favour moiré physics I could accept it, but I would want that discussion of Cao and of Dean and others first, and I do not think it is further ahead than circuit QED on maturity.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks first, with Katori and Ye as a clean two-person attribution, 1e-18 accuracy confirmed in several laboratories, and good timing because of the possible redefinition of the second. He ranked circuit QED fourth and noted that a recent related prize slightly lowers its urgency.
responses.response: Optical lattice clocks are an excellent candidate and I ranked them fifth only because I find the conceptual step slightly smaller than the engineering achievement, which is a matter of taste rather than a flaw. I agree the attribution is cleaner than for most candidates. On urgency I would argue the reverse: the clock result is secure and will remain so whether or not the second is redefined this decade, so the pending redefinition is not a reason to act now, and the 2005 comb prize partly covers the same metrological ground. I would therefore not object to the clocks if the committee prefers them, but I do not accept that the 2025 prize reduces the claim of circuit QED to the same degree, for the reason I gave to Danielsson.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED first and described it as a clean trio with theory from Blais and experiments from Wallraff and Schoelkopf, noting its maturity and its role in nearly every superconducting processor.
responses.response: I agree on the central case and on the trio. I would add one qualification to our shared enthusiasm: two members agreeing on first place is not evidence of merit in itself, and I would rather the case rest on the arguments. The distinction I would insist on is that the prize cites the architecture of strong coupling and dispersive readout, not the transmon or later error-correction demonstrations, which belong to other people and to a later story. If we keep the citation that narrow, the attribution holds; if colleagues want it broader, I would expect Devoret and Girvin to enter the discussion, and that would overflow the three-person limit.

uncertainties: Whether the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes a circuit QED award look like a repeat to the wider committee, or whether the two are distinct enough.
Whether Girvin (and Huang) should have been credited alongside Blais for the 2004 theory proposal, which would crowd the three-person limit.

Whether a theory-and-engineering architecture prize outweighs a discovery-type result such as the Higgs observation or IceCube neutrinos, if the committee leans on the discovery-over-invention criterion.
Attribution within the Higgs and IceCube cases remains unresolved from the material in front of me, so I cannot compare them fairly with circuit QED on that axis.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the credited candidates in B016, B005, or B043 appears among my documented co-authors, supervisors or institutions. My own research is in statistical physics of complex systems rather than quantum circuits, which is a limit on my expertise, not a conflict.
